Researcher Publishes GitLab RCE PoC Letting Authenticated Users Run Commands as Git

The Hacker News
2026-07-25 12 use cases 7 techniques 5 kill-chain phases detected

Security researchers at&nbsp;depthfirst published working exploit code on July 24 for a GitLab flaw that GitLab patched six weeks earlier, on June 10. It runs commands as git on any self-managed 18.11.3 server that has not taken the update. Any authenticated user who can push to a project can run it. The attacker commits a crafted Jupyter notebook and opens its commit diff, which leaks a heap

Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution · Email attachment opened from external sender
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → [LLM] GitLab Puma/Ruby worker (running as git) spawns shell or network tool — Oj .ipynb RCE landing · Office app spawning script/LOLBin child process · Trusted vendor binary / installer launching unusual children

Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → Infostealer — non-browser process accessing browser cookie/login DBs · OAuth consent / suspicious app grant · Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change · LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) · Remote service execution — PsExec / SMB lateral movement
GitLab Puma/Ruby worker (running as git) spawns shell or network tool — Oj .ipynb RCE landing AIExploitation High
Hunts the moment the GitLab notebook-diff RCE chain lands: the long-lived Puma worker (Ruby, running as the git service account) spawns an interpreter or network utility via the forged system() gadget. GitLab's web worker legitimately spawns git/gitaly helpers but never /bin/sh, curl, nc, python, or perl, making this a high-fidelity execution signal for CVE-less Oj 3.13.0-3.17.1 exploitation on self-managed 18.11.3 and the affected 15.2.0-19.0.1 ranges. Rationale: Anchors on the article's specific chain: attacker-controlled .ipynb JSON reaches Oj::Parser.usual.parse inside the long-lived Puma worker and the forged gadget reaches system() to 'connect back as git'. A GitLab web worker spawning sh/curl/nc/python is the exact execution artifact and is otherwise never legitimate for that process. No second-source corroboration available (bug pair shipped by GitLab without CVE/CVSS; not searchable).
ATT&CKT1190 T1059.004
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Custom GitLab server hooks or global git hooks that legitimately shell out from the web worker
  • Admin/maintenance scripts run under the git service account (backup, gitlab-ctl, rake tasks) that spawn curl/wget
  • GitLab integration or webhook helpers invoked by the app that call curl for outbound HTTP
  • Monitoring/agent tooling (e.g. Datadog, node_exporter wrappers) mis-attributed to the ruby parent
  • Container health-check probes exec'ing sh inside the webservice pod
Suppression filter
| where not (ProcessCommandLine has_any ("gitlab-backup","gitlab-ctl","gitaly","/opt/gitlab/embedded/service/gitlab-rails/lib/tasks") or InitiatingProcessCommandLine has "sidekiq")
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the full process tree for the flagged ruby/puma PID on the host — capture child ProcessCommandLine, working dir, and the git user's recent auth. Confirm the parent is a Puma web worker (cmdline 'puma: cluster worker'), not Sidekiq or a legit hook. 2) Contain: isolate the GitLab host/pod, kill the child process, and block egress to any observed remote IP; snapshot memory before reboot. Immediately upgrade the instance to 18.10.8 / 18.11.5 / 19.0.2 (Oj 3.17.3) — no workaround exists. 3) Hunt: review production_json.log for diffs_stream requests referencing .ipynb files, identify the authenticating user/project, pivot on that user's other repos, and check for outbound reverse-shell connections from ruby (see companion C2 UC).
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessCommandLine has "puma" or InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("puma","ruby")
| where FileName in~ ("sh","bash","dash","zsh","nc","ncat","netcat","curl","wget","python","python3","perl","socat")
| where AccountName in~ ("git","gitlab-www","gitlab")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessAccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where ParentProcessName has "puma" or ParentProcessName endswith "/ruby" or ParentProcessName == "ruby"
| where ActingProcessName has_any ("/sh","/bash","/dash","/zsh","/nc","/ncat","/netcat","/curl","/wget","/python","/python3","/perl","/socat")
| where ActorUsername in~ ("git","gitlab-www","gitlab")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ParentProcessName, ParentProcessCommandLine, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: GitLab Puma Worker Spawns Shell or Network Tool (Oj Notebook-Diff RCE)
id: 6b2e9a41-5f3c-4d21-9c7e-2a1b8f0e4c33
description: Detects the GitLab web worker (Ruby/Puma running as git) spawning an interpreter or network utility, consistent with the Oj .ipynb notebook-diff RCE chain landing code execution as git.

| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where (Processes.parent_process_name IN ("ruby","puma") OR Processes.parent_process="*puma*") AND Processes.process_name IN ("sh","bash","dash","zsh","nc","ncat","netcat","curl","wget","python","python3","perl","socat") AND Processes.user IN ("git","gitlab-www","gitlab") by Processes.dest Processes.user Processes.parent_process_name Processes.parent_process Processes.process_name Processes.process | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)` | sort - lastTime
Outbound reverse-shell egress from GitLab Ruby/Puma worker as git — Oj RCE connect-back AICommand & Control Medium
Hunts the C2 stage of the GitLab notebook-diff exploit: after code executes as git, the public PoC makes the Puma worker connect back. This surfaces the GitLab web/Ruby process (git service account) initiating outbound connections to public IPs, which is abnormal for a worker that normally only talks to internal services. Distinct pivot from the process-spawn UC — network shape rather than process tree. Rationale: The article states exploitation 'makes the Puma worker connect back as git', so the git-owned ruby/puma process opening an outbound public connection is the direct C2 artifact. Kept at Medium/hunting because GitLab integrations, webhooks and package proxies also egress from the app — analysts should baseline the destination. Sentinel left empty: no ASIM network table in this tenant carries the initiating process name needed to attribute egress to Puma. No second source available.
ATT&CKT1071 T1190
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • GitLab outbound webhooks / project integrations (Slack, Jira, Jenkins) initiated by the web worker
  • External package registry or mirror pull-through proxying to public endpoints
  • GitLab license/version-check or telemetry calls to GitLab.com
  • Object storage (S3/GCS) reachable over public IPs for artifacts/LFS
  • OmniAuth/SSO metadata or JWKS fetches to external identity providers
Response runbook
1) Triage: resolve the RemoteIP (WHOIS/threat-intel), check whether it matches any configured GitLab integration, mirror, or object-store endpoint. Correlate the connection time against the process-spawn UC and against diffs_stream requests in production_json.log. 2) Contain: block egress to the IP at the firewall, isolate the host, and kill the offending ruby/puma child; preserve netstat/memory before recycling the worker. Patch to 18.10.8/18.11.5/19.0.2. 3) Hunt: enumerate what git can reach (Rails secrets, service creds, CI/CD tokens, internal services) and rotate exposed secrets; review the exploiting user's projects for additional crafted .ipynb notebooks.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessCommandLine has "puma" or InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("puma","ruby")
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName in~ ("git","gitlab-www","gitlab")
| where RemoteIPType == "Public"
| where ActionType == "ConnectionSuccess"
| summarize FirstSeen=min(Timestamp), LastSeen=max(Timestamp), Count=count(), Ports=make_set(RemotePort, 15) by DeviceName, RemoteIP, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by FirstSeen desc
// Microsoft Sentinel — auto-derived from the Defender XDR hunt.
// Requires the Microsoft 365 Defender data connector (streams the
// advanced-hunting tables into Sentinel; Timestamp → TimeGenerated).
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessCommandLine has "puma" or InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("puma","ruby")
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName in~ ("git","gitlab-www","gitlab")
| where RemoteIPType == "Public"
| where ActionType == "ConnectionSuccess"
| summarize FirstSeen=min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen=max(TimeGenerated), Count=count(), Ports=make_set(RemotePort, 15) by DeviceName, RemoteIP, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by FirstSeen desc
#event_simpleName=NetworkConnectIP4 ContextImageFileName=/(ruby|puma)/i
| ConnectionDirection=1
| NOT cidr("10.0.0.0/8", field=RemoteAddressIP4)
| NOT cidr("172.16.0.0/12", field=RemoteAddressIP4)
| NOT cidr("192.168.0.0/16", field=RemoteAddressIP4)
| NOT cidr("127.0.0.0/8", field=RemoteAddressIP4)
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, RemoteAddressIP4, RemotePort, ContextImageFileName], function=count())

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url

Email attachment opened from external sender Delivery High
Attachment delivery + execution by recipient — most common malware initial access.
ATT&CKT1566.001 T1204.002
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Endpoint.Processes EmailAttachmentInfo DeviceProcessEvents
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MalAttachments = EmailAttachmentInfo
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | project NetworkMessageId, RecipientEmailAddress,
              AttachmentFileName = FileName, AttachmentSHA256 = SHA256;
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                      "mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
| join kind=inner MalAttachments on $left.AccountUpn == $right.RecipientEmailAddress
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, AttachmentFileName, AttachmentSHA256
// Sentinel doesn't have an attachment-hash table. Best approximation:
// OfficeActivity Send/Receive activity + correlate to host process spawn.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MailWithAttach = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation in~ ("Send","Receive")
    | where isnotempty(MessageId)
    | project EmailTime = TimeGenerated, MailboxOwnerUPN, Sender,
              Recipients, Subject, MessageId;
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "OUTLOOK.EXE"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine,
          ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

          AND Processes.process_name IN ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")

Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change Actions on Objectives Medium
Threshold detection: many files renamed in short window, often with new extension.
ATT&CKT1486
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem DeviceFileEvents
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(FileName) by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, bin(Timestamp, 1m)
| where files > 200    // empirical: > 200 unique-file renames in 1m by one account on one host
                       //            is well above the P99 of legitimate bulk-tooling
| order by files desc

ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
| where EventType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(TargetFileName)
            by DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, bin(TimeGenerated, 1m)
| where files > 200    // P99 of legit bulk-tooling per-minute rename volume
| order by files desc
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count, dc(Filesystem.file_name) AS files
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where Filesystem.action IN ("modified","renamed")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.user, _time span=1m
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| where files > 200
| sort - files
| tstats summariesonly=false count, dc(Filesystem.file_name) AS files
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where Filesystem.action IN ("modified","renamed")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.user, _time span=1m
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| where files > 200
| sort - files

ATT&CKT1003.001 T1003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceEvents
DeviceEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType == "OpenProcessApiCall"
| where FileName =~ "lsass.exe"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("MsSense.exe","MsMpEng.exe","csrss.exe",
                                          "svchost.exe","wininit.exe","services.exe",
                                          "lsm.exe","SearchProtocolHost.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFolderPath, AccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
// SecurityEvent EventID 4663 = object access. AccessMask 0x10 / 0x40 / 0x1010
// indicate read access to lsass.exe — credential-dump signature. Audit
// Object Access > Audit File System policy required.
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4663
| where ObjectName endswith "\lsass.exe"
| where Account !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ObjectName, ProcessName,
          AccessMask, AccessReason
| order by TimeGenerated desc

For years, phishing campaigns targeting financial institutions followed the same playbook. Victims were tricked into entering usernames and passwords, attackers collected the credentials, and accounts were compromised later when an opportunity arose. That model is changing. Recent investigations into insurance-focused phishing operations reveal a more immediate approach. Instead of harvesting

Actions on Objectives
Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → [LLM] InsureTrap malvertising: Google Ads referrer landing on free-hosting insurance phish · Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution · Email attachment opened from external sender
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → Office app spawning script/LOLBin child process · Fake CAPTCHA / clipboard-injected PowerShell (ClickFix / FakeCaptcha) · Trusted vendor binary / installer launching unusual children
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → Suspicious browser extension installation
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking.
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → [LLM] InsureOTP kit exfiltration: browser connecting to api.telegram.org Bot API · Infostealer — non-browser process accessing browser cookie/login DBs · OAuth consent / suspicious app grant · Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change · LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) · Remote service execution — PsExec / SMB lateral movement
InsureTrap malvertising: Google Ads referrer landing on free-hosting insurance phish AIDelivery Medium
Hunts corporate users who reach a credential-harvesting page hosted on the disposable platforms CTM360 named for the InsureTrap campaign (GitHub Pages, Netlify, Wix, Hostinger, Lovable) via a Google Ads click referrer. This is the campaign's signature initial-access chain: sponsored 'compare car insurance' ads redirecting to look-alike insurer portals on free hosting rather than email/SMS lures. Rationale: Uses the exact delivery vector (Google Ads referrer) and the specific free-hosting platforms CTM360 named for InsureTrap (GitHub Pages/Netlify/Wix/Hostinger/Lovable). Referrer+host on a single proxy row is high-signal; endpoint fallback uses a 90s ad-click->landing correlation. Datadog/Falcon/CloudWatch left empty because HTTP referrer is not carried in FDR DNS/network or the standard Datadog sources. Cross-checked against: • https://www.ctm360.com/reports/insuretrap-fake-insurance-phishing-account-hijacking • https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/ctm360-research-reveals-how-insurance.html
ATT&CKT1583.008 T1566.002 T1204.001
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate small-business insurance broker whose real site is hosted on Netlify/Wix and advertised via Google Ads
  • Marketing landing pages your own org hosts on GitHub Pages/Netlify reached through a Google Ads campaign
  • SaaS product demo/preview sites on lovable.app or netlify.app that users find via sponsored search
  • Ad-tech redirectors that pass a doubleclick referrer to any downstream site the user browses next
Suppression filter
| where not (Url has_any ("<your-corp-brand>.netlify.app","<your-corp-brand>.github.io"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: open the landing Url and referrer; confirm the host is a randomized subdomain with insurance branding (logo/quote workflow) impersonating a known insurer rather than a legitimate business site. 2) Contain: block the specific host/FQDN at the web proxy and DNS, and warn/reset any user who submitted credentials or an OTP on the page. 3) Hunt: pivot on SrcUsername/DeviceId for a follow-on connection to api.telegram.org (see the Telegram exfil UC) and for repeat visits to sibling randomized subdomains on the same free-hosting platform.
let Window = 90s;
let AdClicks = DeviceNetworkEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
    | where RemoteUrl has_any ("googleadservices.com","googleads.g.doubleclick.net","g.doubleclick.net")
    | project DeviceId, AdTime = Timestamp;
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
| where RemoteUrl has_any ("github.io","netlify.app","netlify.com","wixsite.com","hostingersite.com","lovable.app","lovableproject.com","lovable.dev")
| join kind=inner AdClicks on DeviceId
| where Timestamp between (AdTime .. AdTime + Window)
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, LandingUrl = RemoteUrl, RemoteIP, AdTime, DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, AdTime)
| order by Timestamp desc
ImWebSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where Url has_any ("github.io","netlify.app","netlify.com","wixsite.com","hostingersite.com","lovable.app","lovableproject.com","lovable.dev")
| where HttpRequestHeaderReferer has_any ("googleadservices.com","doubleclick.net","googleads")
| project TimeGenerated, SrcIpAddr, SrcUsername, HttpHostName, Url, Referer = HttpRequestHeaderReferer, HttpRequestHeaderUserAgent, DstIpAddr
| order by TimeGenerated desc

InsureOTP kit exfiltration: browser connecting to api.telegram.org Bot API AIActions on Objectives High
Hunts a browser process making an outbound connection/DNS lookup to api.telegram.org — the Bot API host the InsureOTP kit uses to relay harvested credentials and OTP codes to operators in real time. Legitimate Telegram web clients talk to web.telegram.org/Telegram DCs, not the Bot API host, so a browser reaching api.telegram.org is a strong client-side phishing-exfil indicator. Rationale: api.telegram.org is the concrete Bot API host CTM360 tied to the InsureOTP kit's exfiltration, corroborated as a phishing-kit exfil channel by Securelist and the SOCFortress FEMITBOT writeup. Browser-initiated traffic to it (vs. web.telegram.org for legit clients) is inherently anomalous, giving a low-FP alerting-grade signal. Cross-checked against: • https://securelist.com/telegram-phishing-services/109383/ • https://socfortress.medium.com/the-telegram-trap-inside-the-sophisticated-femitbot-fraud-network-8b310c8c9df8 • https://www.ctm360.com/reports/insuretrap-fake-insurance-phishing-account-hijacking
ATT&CKT1567 T1102 T1111
Data sourcesNetwork_Resolution.DNS
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Developer testing a legitimate Telegram bot from a browser-based API console or Swagger/Postman-in-browser session
  • Internal IT/marketing automation dashboards that embed Telegram Bot API calls and are opened in a browser
  • Browser extension that legitimately integrates a personal Telegram bot for notifications
  • Security researcher or this very hunt loading api.telegram.org documentation/endpoints in a browser
Suppression filter
| where DeviceName !in~ ("dev-automation-host", "marketing-notify-host")
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the tab/URL that drove the connection and whether the initiating browser had just loaded a free-hosting insurance page (correlate with the InsureTrap malvertising UC on the same device/user). 2) Contain: force-reset the user's credentials and revoke sessions for any insurer/personal accounts entered, and block api.telegram.org egress for standard user browsers at the proxy. 3) Hunt: sweep all endpoints for browser->api.telegram.org, extract the visited phishing host from proxy logs, and block sibling randomized domains; check whether harvested identity data (policy/ID documents) warrants fraud/notification workflows.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where RemoteUrl has "api.telegram.org"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe","iexplore.exe")
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| summarize FirstSeen = min(Timestamp), LastSeen = max(Timestamp), Conns = count(), any(RemoteIP) by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, RemoteUrl
| order by LastSeen desc
ImDnsActivity
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where DnsQuery =~ "api.telegram.org" or DnsQuery endswith ".api.telegram.org"
| summarize FirstSeen = min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen = max(TimeGenerated), Lookups = count() by SrcIpAddr, SrcHostname, SrcUsername, DnsQuery
| order by LastSeen desc

title: Infostealer - Non-Browser Process Accessing Browser Credential Stores
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d01
status: experimental
description: |
    Stealers (RedLine, Lumma, Vidar, Atomic) read Login Data / cookies
    SQLite databases from Chrome/Edge/Firefox profile directories. Any
    non-browser process touching these files is a high-fidelity signal.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1539/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1555/003/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1539
    - attack.t1555.003
    - attack.credential-access
logsource:
    category: file_access
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_path:
        TargetFilename|contains:
            - '\Google\Chrome\User Data\'
            - '\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\'
            - '\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\'
    selection_file:
        TargetFilename|endswith:
            - '\Login Data'
            - '\Cookies'
            - '\logins.json'
            - '\cookies.sqlite'
    filter_browser:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\chrome.exe'
            - '\msedge.exe'
            - '\firefox.exe'
            - '\brave.exe'
            - '\opera.exe'
    condition: selection_path and selection_file and not filter_browser
falsepositives:
    - Backup utilities reading user profile files
    - Browser sync agents from non-stock vendors
level: high
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where (Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Cookies*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\logins.json*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\cookies.sqlite*")
      AND NOT Filesystem.process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.process_name, Filesystem.file_path, Filesystem.user
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where (Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Cookies*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\logins.json*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\cookies.sqlite*")
      AND NOT Filesystem.process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.process_name, Filesystem.file_path, Filesystem.user
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats summariesonly=false count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",

                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time
Email attachment opened from external sender Delivery High
Attachment delivery + execution by recipient — most common malware initial access.
ATT&CKT1566.001 T1204.002
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Endpoint.Processes EmailAttachmentInfo DeviceProcessEvents
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MalAttachments = EmailAttachmentInfo
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | project NetworkMessageId, RecipientEmailAddress,
              AttachmentFileName = FileName, AttachmentSHA256 = SHA256;
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                      "mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
| join kind=inner MalAttachments on $left.AccountUpn == $right.RecipientEmailAddress
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, AttachmentFileName, AttachmentSHA256
// Sentinel doesn't have an attachment-hash table. Best approximation:
// OfficeActivity Send/Receive activity + correlate to host process spawn.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MailWithAttach = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation in~ ("Send","Receive")
    | where isnotempty(MessageId)
    | project EmailTime = TimeGenerated, MailboxOwnerUPN, Sender,
              Recipients, Subject, MessageId;
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "OUTLOOK.EXE"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine,
          ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change Actions on Objectives Medium
Threshold detection: many files renamed in short window, often with new extension.
ATT&CKT1486
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem DeviceFileEvents
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(FileName) by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, bin(Timestamp, 1m)
| where files > 200    // empirical: > 200 unique-file renames in 1m by one account on one host
                       //            is well above the P99 of legitimate bulk-tooling
| order by files desc

ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
| where EventType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(TargetFileName)
            by DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, bin(TimeGenerated, 1m)
| where files > 200    // P99 of legit bulk-tooling per-minute rename volume
| order by files desc
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count, dc(Filesystem.file_name) AS files
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where Filesystem.action IN ("modified","renamed")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.user, _time span=1m
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| where files > 200
| sort - files
| tstats summariesonly=false count, dc(Filesystem.file_name) AS files
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where Filesystem.action IN ("modified","renamed")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.user, _time span=1m
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| where files > 200
| sort - files
LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) Actions on Objectives High
Mimikatz, comsvcs.dll MiniDump, or any non-Windows process opening LSASS.
ATT&CKT1003.001 T1003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceEvents
DeviceEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType == "OpenProcessApiCall"
| where FileName =~ "lsass.exe"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("MsSense.exe","MsMpEng.exe","csrss.exe",

| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine,

// SecurityEvent EventID 4663 = object access. AccessMask 0x10 / 0x40 / 0x1010

SecurityEvent

| where ObjectName endswith "\lsass.exe"
| where Account !endswith "$"

Cl0p hex-named JSP web shell dropped under /Windchill/login/ (CVE-2026-12569) AIInstallation Medium
Hunts for creation of hex-named JSP web shells in the PTC Windchill/FlexPLM login directory, the post-exploitation payload of CVE-2026-12569 unauthenticated deserialization RCE. Files follow the pattern /Windchill/login/[0-9a-f]{16}.jsp and are written by the Java/Tomcat web tier — never a legitimate operation. Rationale: Uses the article's exact web-shell path /Windchill/login/ and the corroborated [0-9a-f]{16}.jsp naming pattern plus the published SHA256 — a JSP file created in the login directory has no legitimate cause, making this near-zero FP. Cross-checked against: • https://ransom-isac.org/blog/clop-windchill-flexplm-exploitation/ • https://www.helpnetsecurity.com/2026/06/29/ptc-windchill-cve-2026-12569-exploited/ • https://www.ptc.com/en/about/trust-center/advisory-center/active-advisories/windchill-flexplm-rce-vulnerability • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/clop-ransomware-targets-windchill-flexplm-in-data-theft-attacks/
ATT&CKT1505.003 T1190
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate Windchill patch/hotfix deployment adding new JSP files to the web app (but not under login/ with hex names)
  • Windchill build/deploy pipeline unpacking WAR files into the app directory
  • Security scanner or IR tooling writing test .jsp files during a pentest of the PLM server
  • Backup/restore of the Windchill webapps tree re-creating existing JSP files
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("java.exe","javaw.exe","tomcat9.exe","tomcat10.exe","tomcat.exe","w3wp.exe") or FileName matches regex @"^[0-9a-f]{16}\.jsp$"
Response runbook
1) Triage: retrieve the JSP file at the flagged path and hash it; compare to 55a1eb4c...; open the file — Cl0p shells contain runtime command-exec logic (Runtime.exec/ProcessBuilder). Confirm the writing process is java/tomcat. 2) Contain: isolate the Windchill/FlexPLM host from the network, preserve the web shell for forensics, and confirm CVE-2026-12569 patch (PTC June 2026 fix) is applied; rotate any service/DB credentials reachable from the app. 3) Hunt: pull Tomcat access logs for POSTs to the FlexPLM WSDL endpoint and /Windchill/login servlet from the 4 Cl0p IPs; search all Windchill hosts for additional hex-named JSPs and flst.txt enumeration output.

| where Timestamp > ago(30d)

| where FolderPath has @"\Windchill\login\" or FolderPath contains "/Windchill/login/"

| project Timestamp, DeviceName, FolderPath, FileName, SHA256, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessAccountName
| order by Timestamp desc

| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, TargetFilePath, TargetFileName, TargetFileSHA256, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

PTC Windchill Java/Tomcat web tier spawning OS command shell (web shell RCE) AIExploitation High
Hunts the RCE execution stage of CVE-2026-12569: the Windchill Java/Tomcat process spawning cmd/powershell/whoami/net and other discovery binaries via the deployed JSP web shell. A PLM application server should never spawn interactive OS command interpreters. Rationale: Ties the article's Windchill RCE to its concrete host behaviour: the Java/Tomcat web tier (confirmed exploited process) spawning command shells is the observable of 'remote command execution' via the JSP shell — a PLM app server has no legitimate reason to launch cmd/whoami/net. Cross-checked against: • https://ransom-isac.org/blog/clop-windchill-flexplm-exploitation/ • https://www.helpnetsecurity.com/2026/06/29/ptc-windchill-cve-2026-12569-exploited/ • https://www.securityweek.com/first-ever-exploitation-of-ptc-windchill-vulnerability-discovered-in-the-wild/
ATT&CKT1059.003 T1505.003 T1190
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Windchill scheduled tasks or method-server jobs legitimately shelling out to run configured scripts (net use for file shares, hostname checks)
  • Administrator running diagnostic scripts under the Tomcat service account
  • Windchill installer/upgrade invoking cmd.exe to set environment or register services
  • Monitoring agents launched by the JVM that call ipconfig/hostname for inventory
Suppression filter
| where not (ProcessCommandLine has_any ("WindchillDS","wt.method","windchill start","windchill stop") and AccountName !endswith "$" and InitiatingProcessCommandLine has "Windchill")
Response runbook
1) Triage: inspect the child ProcessCommandLine — enumeration (whoami/net group/systeminfo) or download (certutil/bitsadmin) from the Tomcat account is high-confidence RCE; capture the parent Java command line and Windchill install path. 2) Contain: isolate the host, kill the offending process tree, and block outbound to the 4 Cl0p IPs at the perimeter; freeze the Tomcat service account. 3) Hunt: correlate to hex-named JSP creation (UC1) and flst.txt writes on the same host in the preceding minutes; sweep peer PLM servers for identical java→cmd parentage.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("java.exe","javaw.exe","tomcat9.exe","tomcat10.exe","tomcat.exe","java")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","whoami.exe","net.exe","net1.exe","systeminfo.exe","ipconfig.exe","hostname.exe","tasklist.exe","certutil.exe","bitsadmin.exe","cscript.exe","wscript.exe","sh","bash","whoami","id")
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, FolderPath, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("java.exe","javaw.exe","tomcat9.exe","tomcat10.exe","tomcat.exe")
| where ActingProcessName has_any ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","whoami.exe","net.exe","net1.exe","systeminfo.exe","ipconfig.exe","hostname.exe","tasklist.exe","certutil.exe","bitsadmin.exe","cscript.exe","wscript.exe")
| where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ParentProcessName, ParentProcessCommandLine, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Network connections to Cl0p CVE-2026-12569 C2 / staging infrastructure AICommand & Control Medium
Flags any host communicating with the four Ransom-ISAC/PTC-published Cl0p IPs used to exploit and exfiltrate from Windchill/FlexPLM, with 5.180.41.35 prioritised as confirmed C2/staging. Catches inbound exploitation source IPs and outbound data-staging egress from the PLM DMZ. Rationale: Uses the four IPs jointly confirmed by Ransom-ISAC and the PTC advisory; 5.180.41.35 is flagged by Ransom-ISAC as priority-block C2/staging, so any match on a PLM host is high-fidelity regardless of direction. Cross-checked against: • https://ransom-isac.org/blog/clop-windchill-flexplm-exploitation/ • https://www.ptc.com/en/about/trust-center/advisory-center/active-advisories/windchill-flexplm-rce-vulnerability • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/clop-ransomware-targets-windchill-flexplm-in-data-theft-attacks/

Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the internal host and the initiating process; if it is the Windchill/Tomcat server or the connection is inbound to the PLM login/WSDL ports, treat as active exploitation. 2) Contain: block all four IPs at firewall/proxy, isolate any Windchill host that talked to them, and capture NetFlow bytes_out to estimate exfil volume to 5.180.41.35. 3) Hunt: pivot on the host to UC1 (web shell) and UC2 (java→cmd) events; review Tomcat access logs for the source IPs hitting the FlexPLM WSDL endpoint; scope other externally-exposed PLM assets.

Windchill filesystem-enumeration artifact flst.txt written by web tier (CVE-2026-12569 discovery) AIActions on Objectives Medium
Hunts creation of the flst.txt filesystem-enumeration output file that Cl0p affiliates generate post-exploitation on Windchill/FlexPLM servers to stage engineering/design data for theft. High fidelity when written by the Java/Tomcat web tier or a shell it spawned, or when it lands under the Windchill install tree. Rationale: flst.txt is the specific enumeration-output filename attributed to this campaign by Ransom-ISAC; scoping the writer to the Java/Tomcat web tier or the Windchill path removes generic flst.txt noise and pins it to the exploited PLM server. Cross-checked against: • https://ransom-isac.org/blog/clop-windchill-flexplm-exploitation/ • https://gbhackers.com/cl0p-targets-internet-exposed-windchill/
ATT&CKT1083 T1074.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A developer or admin coincidentally naming a legitimate file listing flst.txt on the server
  • Windchill batch/report jobs that emit a text file listing under the install directory
  • Backup or file-integrity tooling that produces per-directory listings named flst.txt
  • Third-party CAD/PLM integration script writing an inventory file with the same name
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$" and (FolderPath has @"\Windchill\" or InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("java.exe","javaw.exe","tomcat9.exe","tomcat10.exe"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: open flst.txt — a recursive listing of engineering/design directories written by the Tomcat account confirms Cl0p staging; note the enumerated paths (they reveal the intended exfil target set). 2) Contain: isolate the host, preserve flst.txt and any adjacent staged archives, and revoke the Tomcat service account's access to file shares referenced in the listing. 3) Hunt: correlate with UC1/UC2 on the same host and with outbound bytes to the Cl0p IPs (UC3); search all PLM servers for flst.txt and for large archive files created shortly after by the same process.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where ActionType == "FileCreated"
| where FileName =~ "flst.txt"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("java.exe","javaw.exe","tomcat9.exe","tomcat10.exe","tomcat.exe","cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe")
    or FolderPath has @"\Windchill\" or FolderPath contains "/Windchill/"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, FolderPath, FileName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessParentFileName, InitiatingProcessAccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventType == "FileCreated"
| where TargetFileName =~ "flst.txt"
| where ActingProcessName has_any ("java.exe","javaw.exe","tomcat9.exe","tomcat10.exe","tomcat.exe","cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe")
    or TargetFilePath has @"\Windchill\" or TargetFilePath contains "/Windchill/"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, TargetFilePath, TargetFileName, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, ActorUsername
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```

     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",

Email attachment opened from external sender Delivery High
Attachment delivery + execution by recipient — most common malware initial access.
ATT&CKT1566.001 T1204.002
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Endpoint.Processes EmailAttachmentInfo DeviceProcessEvents
let LookbackDays = 7d;

    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)

// Sentinel doesn't have an attachment-hash table. Best approximation:
// OfficeActivity Send/Receive activity + correlate to host process spawn.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MailWithAttach = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation in~ ("Send","Receive")
    | where isnotempty(MessageId)
    | project EmailTime = TimeGenerated, MailboxOwnerUPN, Sender,

SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "OUTLOOK.EXE"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"

   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"

          ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

DeviceProcessEvents

Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change Actions on Objectives Medium
Threshold detection: many files renamed in short window, often with new extension.
ATT&CKT1486
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem DeviceFileEvents
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(FileName) by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, bin(Timestamp, 1m)
| where files > 200    // empirical: > 200 unique-file renames in 1m by one account on one host
                       //            is well above the P99 of legitimate bulk-tooling
| order by files desc

ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
| where EventType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(TargetFileName)
            by DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, bin(TimeGenerated, 1m)
| where files > 200    // P99 of legit bulk-tooling per-minute rename volume
| order by files desc
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count, dc(Filesystem.file_name) AS files
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where Filesystem.action IN ("modified","renamed")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.user, _time span=1m
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| where files > 200
| sort - files
| tstats summariesonly=false count, dc(Filesystem.file_name) AS files
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where Filesystem.action IN ("modified","renamed")

ATT&CKT1003.001 T1003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceEvents
DeviceEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType == "OpenProcessApiCall"
| where FileName =~ "lsass.exe"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("MsSense.exe","MsMpEng.exe","csrss.exe",
                                          "svchost.exe","wininit.exe","services.exe",

| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFolderPath, AccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
// SecurityEvent EventID 4663 = object access. AccessMask 0x10 / 0x40 / 0x1010
// indicate read access to lsass.exe — credential-dump signature. Audit
// Object Access > Audit File System policy required.
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4663
| where ObjectName endswith "\lsass.exe"
| where Account !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ObjectName, ProcessName,
          AccessMask, AccessReason
| order by TimeGenerated desc

File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match Installation High
Match SHA256/SHA1/MD5 named in the article against EDR file/process telemetry.
ATT&CKT1027
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem Endpoint.Processes DeviceFileEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Pre-filter each table BEFORE the union — the engine cannot push
// predicates across `union`, and DeviceFileEvents lacks ProcessCommandLine
// (Initiating only) so column-projection has to differ per side.
union
    ( DeviceFileEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("55a1eb4c2d3da04376df39d7ba832569c6af1a37a0cf2b95f754ac898023a30c") or SHA1 in~ ("55a1eb4c2d3da04376df39d7ba832569c6af1a37a0cf2b95f754ac898023a30c") or MD5 in~ ("55a1eb4c2d3da04376df39d7ba832569c6af1a37a0cf2b95f754ac898023a30c")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = InitiatingProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceFileEvents" ),
    ( DeviceProcessEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where AccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("55a1eb4c2d3da04376df39d7ba832569c6af1a37a0cf2b95f754ac898023a30c") or SHA1 in~ ("55a1eb4c2d3da04376df39d7ba832569c6af1a37a0cf2b95f754ac898023a30c") or MD5 in~ ("55a1eb4c2d3da04376df39d7ba832569c6af1a37a0cf2b95f754ac898023a30c")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = ProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceProcessEvents" )
| order by Timestamp desc

// Pre-filter both ASIM tables before the union — same pattern as the
// Defender version so the engine can push hash predicates per-side.
let BadHashes = dynamic(["55a1eb4c2d3da04376df39d7ba832569c6af1a37a0cf2b95f754ac898023a30c"]);
union
    ( ImFileEvent
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where TargetFileSHA256 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileSHA1 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileMD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType,
                  TargetFileName, TargetFilePath, TargetFileSHA256,
                  Cmd = ActingProcessName, Source = "ImFileEvent" ),
    ( ImProcessCreate
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ (BadHashes) or SHA1 in~ (BadHashes) or MD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileName = TargetProcessName, TargetFilePath = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileSHA256 = SHA256,
                  Cmd = TargetProcessCommandLine, Source = "ImProcessCreate" )
| order by TimeGenerated desc

The Hacker News
2026-07-25 15 use cases 7 techniques 4 kill-chain phases detected

The operators of the DevMan ransomware-as-a-service (RaaS) scheme are maintaining a dedicated web platform that offers affiliates the ability to build payloads, oversee earnings, and manage various aspects related to victims. Swiss cybersecurity company PRODAFT is tracking the centrally administered RaaS operation under the name Funky Mantis. "The portal combined build generation, finance,

Actions on Objectives
Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution · Email attachment opened from external sender
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → Office app spawning script/LOLBin child process · Trusted vendor binary / installer launching unusual children
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] DevMan/Funky Mantis locker execution by known SHA256/MD5 hash · Suspicious browser extension installation · RMM tool installed by non-IT user — remote-access utility for hands-on-keyboard · File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking.
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → [LLM] DevMan ransomware encryption artifacts: .devman extension and deterministic ransom note · [LLM] DevMan pre-encryption recovery inhibition and event-log clearing · Infostealer — non-browser process accessing browser cookie/login DBs · Remote service execution — PsExec / SMB lateral movement · OAuth consent / suspicious app grant · Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change · LSASS process access / dump (credential theft)
DevMan/Funky Mantis locker execution by known SHA256/MD5 hash AIInstallation Medium
Hunts execution of the DevMan (DragonForce-lineage) ransomware payload by the specific SHA256/MD5 hashes published by PRODAFT. Because DevMan is deployed hands-on-keyboard after broker access, any host running these binaries is an active encryption event, not a test. Rationale: Uses the two SHA256 and one MD5 hash published by PRODAFT for the DevMan locker; a hash match on process execution is unambiguous for an actively-deployed RaaS payload. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/prodaft/malware-ioc • https://any.run/cybersecurity-blog/devman-ransomware-analysis/ • https://malpedia.caad.fkie.fraunhofer.de/details/win.devman
ATT&CKT1486 T1204.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Malware-analysis sandbox / detonation VM intentionally running the sample
  • IR or red-team retained sample copied to a jump box for reverse engineering
  • EDR test/validation exercise seeding known-bad hashes
  • Threat-intel researcher workstation with sample repository indexed by AV
Suppression filter
| where not (DeviceName has_any ("SANDBOX","MALLAB","ANALYSIS"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the host is production (not a sandbox/analysis VM) and pull parent process + logon session for the hash hit — identify how the binary landed. 2) Contain: network-isolate the host immediately, kill the process, and disable the executing account; DevMan is hands-on-keyboard so treat as live encryption. 3) Hunt: sweep for the `.devman` extension and ransom note `e47qfsnz2trbkhnt.devman` across shares, check for VPN logins by service/backup accounts, and look for the same hashes staged on other hosts via SMB.

| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where SHA256 in~ ("df5ab9015833023a03f92a797e20196672c1d6525501a9f9a94a45b0904c7403","018494565257ef2b6a4e68f1c3e7573b87fc53bd5828c9c5127f31d37ea964f8")
    or MD5 =~ "e84270afa3030b48dc9e0c53a35c65aa"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, FolderPath, ProcessCommandLine, SHA256, MD5, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where SHA256 in~ ("df5ab9015833023a03f92a797e20196672c1d6525501a9f9a94a45b0904c7403","018494565257ef2b6a4e68f1c3e7573b87fc53bd5828c9c5127f31d37ea964f8")
    or MD5 =~ "e84270afa3030b48dc9e0c53a35c65aa"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, TargetProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, SHA256, MD5
| order by TimeGenerated desc

DevMan ransomware encryption artifacts: .devman extension and deterministic ransom note AIActions on Objectives High
Hunts mass creation/rename of files with the DevMan-specific `.devman` extension and the builder-flaw ransom note filename `e47qfsnz2trbkhnt.devman`. Thresholding on volume per host in a short window distinguishes encryption from a one-off file. Rationale: The `.devman` extension and the deterministic note name `e47qfsnz2trbkhnt.devman` (builder flaw that re-encrypts its own notes) are DevMan-specific and independently confirmed by ANY.RUN and Malpedia; volume threshold separates encryption from noise. Cross-checked against: • https://any.run/cybersecurity-blog/devman-ransomware-analysis/ • https://medium.com/@anyrun/devman-ransomware-overview-32600d4da684 • https://malpedia.caad.fkie.fraunhofer.de/details/win.devman
ATT&CKT1486
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A user or app legitimately creating a file that coincidentally ends in .devman (extremely rare, non-threshold branch mitigates)
  • Backup/restore tooling replaying previously-encrypted .devman files during a recovery drill
  • EDR retro-scan re-indexing an old encrypted directory generating burst file events
  • Security team detonating a sample in a monitored share
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("veeam.backup.shell.exe","wbengine.exe","backup.exe")
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the >50-file burst is on a production endpoint/share and identify the InitiatingProcess writing the `.devman` files. 2) Contain: isolate the host, kill the writing process, revoke the account, and disconnect mapped drives/SMB sessions to stop lateral encryption. 3) Hunt: enumerate all hosts touching the same share, check for the known payload hashes, event-log clearing and shadow-copy deletion (see companion UC), and service/backup-account VPN logins that likely delivered access.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where ActionType in ("FileCreated","FileRenamed")
| where FileName endswith ".devman"
| summarize FileCount = dcount(FolderPath), Note = countif(FileName =~ "e47qfsnz2trbkhnt.devman"), Proc = any(InitiatingProcessFileName), Cmd = any(InitiatingProcessCommandLine), FirstSeen = min(Timestamp) by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, bin(Timestamp, 5m)
| where FileCount > 50 or Note > 0    // >50 encrypted files in 5m OR the deterministic ransom note appears
| order by FirstSeen desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventType in ("FileCreated","FileRenamed","FileModified")
| where TargetFileName endswith ".devman"
| summarize FileCount = dcount(TargetFilePath), Note = countif(TargetFileName =~ "e47qfsnz2trbkhnt.devman"), Proc = any(ActingProcessName), FirstSeen = min(TimeGenerated) by DvcHostname, ActorUsername, bin(TimeGenerated, 5m)
| where FileCount > 50 or Note > 0
| order by FirstSeen desc
title: DevMan Ransomware Deterministic Ransom Note File Creation
id: 2f8c4d13-7a05-4e6b-9c21-84be1f3a7d60
description: Detects creation of the DevMan builder-flaw ransom note e47qfsnz2trbkhnt.devman
references:
  - https://any.run/cybersecurity-blog/devman-ransomware-analysis/
  - https://malpedia.caad.fkie.fraunhofer.de/details/win.devman
author: SOC Detection Engineering
date: 2026/07/26
tags:
