OpenAM/Tomcat Java process spawning a shell — post-deserialization RCE (CVE-2026-62263) AIExploitation High
Hunts the OpenAM JVM (java/java.exe under Tomcat/catalina) spawning a command interpreter or download tool — the payload-execution stage after the WebAuthn gadget chain fires during readObject(). An IAM/SSO appliance's Java process spawning cmd/powershell/sh/curl is abnormal and high-fidelity for RCE. Rationale: Grounded in the article's sink (WebAuthn readObject/readResolve executes during readObject() before any assertion check) and the affected package org.openidentityplatform.openam. The parent-context filter (openam/catalina/tomcat/org.openidentityplatform in the JVM cmdline) pins this to the OpenAM appliance rather than any JVM, and pairing it with a shell/downloader child is the classic Java-deser RCE process shape. Cross-platform (java on Linux, java.exe on Windows) since OpenAM commonly runs on Tomcat/Linux. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-gf8h-gq53-288j • https://advisories.gitlab.com/maven/org.openidentityplatform.openam/openam-auth-webauthn/CVE-2026-45051/ • https://vulnerability.circl.lu/vuln/ghsa-6c99-87fr-6q7r
ATT&CKT1059.004 T1059.001 T1190
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Tomcat startup/shutdown wrappers where catalina.sh/java invokes 'sh -c' during normal service lifecycle
  • OpenAM plugin or scripted auth module that legitimately calls Runtime.exec for a health-check or LDAP helper script
  • Sysadmin running diagnostics under the tomcat/openam service account (whoami, curl to an internal health URL)
  • Monitoring/backup agent shelling out from the JVM for metrics collection
Suppression filter
| where not (ProcessCommandLine has_any ("catalina.sh start","catalina.sh stop","catalina.sh run","-version","/usr/bin/id -u","/healthcheck","/monitoring/"))
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: Inspect the child ProcessCommandLine — decode any base64/encoded command, and check whether it is a known startup script (catalina.sh) or a recon command (whoami, id, curl to attacker host). Correlate the timestamp against UC1 hits (serialized payload to /json/authenticate) on the same host. 2) CONTAIN: Isolate the OpenAM host, kill the offending child and its descendants, and rotate OpenAM service-account and any credentials the JVM could read (LDAP bind, datastore, secrets). 3) HUNT: Search for webshells under the Tomcat webapps dir, new persistence (cron, systemd, Run keys), outbound C2 from the java process, and lateral auth from the OpenAM host; confirm the fix (openam-auth-webauthn > 16.1.1) is deployed everywhere.

Node.js host process spawning OS shell (Nunjucks SSTI child_process.execSync RCE) AIExploitation Medium
Hunts a Node.js runtime process spawning cmd.exe/powershell or a Unix shell, the direct result of an attacker-controlled .prompty template abusing @prompty/core's Nunjucks renderer to reach global.process.mainModule.require('child_process').execSync(). This is article-specific because the RCE terminates in a node→shell parent/child chain that the vulnerable renderer produces. Rationale: Anchored on the corroborated Nunjucks RCE payload chain (range.constructor -> global.process.mainModule.require('child_process').execSync) whose default execSync behaviour spawns cmd.exe /d /s /c on Windows and /bin/sh -c on Linux, producing a node->shell parent/child pair. Cross-checked PayloadsAllTheThings and HackTricks SSTI-JS references plus the GHSA advisory. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-w28w-gp39-m4p6 • https://github.com/swisskyrepo/PayloadsAllTheThings/blob/master/Server%20Side%20Template%20Injection/JavaScript.md • https://hacktricks.wiki/en/pentesting-web/ssti-server-side-template-injection/index.html
ATT&CKT1190 T1059.003 T1059.004
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate Node build tooling (npm/yarn/webpack) invoking cmd.exe /c or /bin/sh -c for lifecycle scripts
  • Electron or CLI apps built on Node that shell out to system utilities by design
  • node-based process managers (pm2, nodemon) restarting apps via a shell
  • CI/CD runners executing shell steps under a Node orchestrator
  • Developer workstations running local server frameworks that exec git/openssl via child_process
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("npm-cli.js","yarn.js","webpack","nodemon","pm2","node-gyp") or ProcessCommandLine has_any ("npm run","prepare","postinstall","node_modules\\.bin"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the full child command line and InitiatingProcessCommandLine — a benign build shows npm/yarn lifecycle strings; malicious shows ad-hoc recon (whoami, id, curl, /dev/tcp reverse shells) or base64. Check whether the node process was serving/rendering .prompty content. 2) Contain: isolate the host, kill the node PID, and block outbound to any IP the spawned shell contacted; snapshot for IR. 3) Hunt: confirm @prompty/core version on the host (UC2), review recently written/downloaded .prompty files for constructor/prototype/child_process tokens, and pivot on the same node process for further shell spawns or network egress.

Vulnerable @prompty/core package present in node_modules (GHSA-w28w-gp39-m4p6 exposure) AIDelivery Medium
Surfaces hosts and build images where the vulnerable @prompty/core npm package is installed by matching its node_modules folder path. Directly implements the advisory's remediation-triage guidance to locate the package before an untrusted .prompty template can trigger SSTI-to-RCE. Rationale: Uses the exact vulnerable package coordinate from the advisory (npm @prompty/core, <=0.1.4 and <=2.0.0-beta.4) matched via its canonical node_modules/@prompty/core install path, directly serving the advisory's 'check whether @prompty/core is present in manifests, lockfiles, or build images' remediation step. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-w28w-gp39-m4p6
ATT&CKT1190 T1195.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Hosts already upgraded to patched @prompty/core 2.0.0-beta.5+ (path alone cannot confirm version — verify package.json)
  • Legitimate developer workstations that intentionally depend on @prompty/core
  • CI/CD build agents that transiently install the package during pipeline runs
  • Container image layers cached on a node showing the folder without runtime use
  • Security researchers/AV quarantine copies of the package under node_modules
Response runbook
1) Triage: on each hit, read node_modules/@prompty/core/package.json (or the lockfile) to confirm the installed version is <=0.1.4 or between 2.0.0-alpha.1 and 2.0.0-beta.4 — patched builds are 2.0.0-beta.5+. 2) Contain: for confirmed-vulnerable production/internet-facing services that render community/cloned/LLM-generated .prompty files, prioritize upgrading to 2.0.0-beta.5 and restrict rendering to trusted templates. 3) Hunt: pivot each vulnerable host into UC1 (node->shell) over the same window, and review recently created/downloaded .prompty files for constructor/prototype/process/child_process traversal tokens.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FolderPath has "node_modules"
| where FolderPath contains @"\@prompty\core" or FolderPath contains "/@prompty/core"
| summarize FirstSeen=min(Timestamp), LastSeen=max(Timestamp), Files=make_set(FileName, 25) by DeviceName, FolderPath, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by LastSeen desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where TargetFilePath has "node_modules"
| where TargetFilePath contains @"\@prompty\core" or TargetFilePath contains "/@prompty/core"
| summarize FirstSeen=min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen=max(TimeGenerated), Files=make_set(TargetFileName, 25) by DvcHostname, TargetFilePath, ActorUsername
| order by LastSeen desc

Velocity.js SSTI RCE payload (constructor.constructor→child_process) in HTTP request AIDelivery High
Hunts inbound HTTP requests carrying the velocityjs template-injection RCE payload described in GHSA-7gfh-x38p-prh3: the property-read chain to the Function constructor plus a child_process command exec. Targets apps that render attacker-controlled Velocity templates (velocityjs ≤2.1.6) at the web/delivery layer where the payload is still visible on the wire. Rationale: Uses the exact exploit-chain strings from the PoC (constructor.constructor, process.mainModule, child_process, #set( / URL-encoded %23set() which are not present in normal Velocity rendering, giving high specificity at the delivery layer. Cross-checked against the prior fix advisory GHSA-j658-c2gf-x6pq (CVE-2026-44966) and the canonical JS-SSTI payload shape in PayloadsAllTheThings. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-j658-c2gf-x6pq • https://github.com/swisskyrepo/PayloadsAllTheThings/blob/master/Server%20Side%20Template%20Injection/JavaScript.md • https://github.com/shepherdwind/velocity.js/pull/192
ATT&CKT1190 T1059.007
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Authorized vulnerability scanners (Nessus/Qualys/Nuclei) firing SSTI templates against the app
  • Contracted penetration test or bug-bounty researcher probing template injection
  • Internal AppSec CI/CD DAST scans (Burp/ZAP) hitting the endpoint
  • A benign field/parameter legitimately containing the literal string 'child_process' (e.g. a code-snippet paste or docs form) with no Velocity markers
  • Security awareness/red-team exercises replaying known SSTI payloads
Suppression filter
| where not(csUserAgent has_any ("Nessus","Qualys","Nuclei","Burp","ZAP","Nikto"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the full request (URI, body, User-Agent, source IP) and confirm the payload contains a Velocity marker (#set / %23set) alongside constructor.constructor or child_process — a raw 'child_process' with no template syntax is likely benign. Check scStatus: a 200/500 suggests the template actually rendered. 2) Contain: if source IP is not an approved scanner, block it at the WAF/edge and confirm the app's velocityjs version — upgrade to 2.1.7+ immediately if ≤2.1.6. 3) Hunt: pivot to the same host's endpoint telemetry (UC 'node process spawning shell') for the ~5 min after the request to confirm code execution; review inbound requests from the same IP for other SSTI variants and check for outbound egress from the node process.
W3CIISLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| extend Req = strcat(csUriStem, "?", csUriQuery)
| where Req contains "constructor.constructor" or Req contains "child_process" or Req contains "process.mainModule" or Req contains "mainModule" or Req contains "%23set(" or Req contains "#set("
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, sSiteName, cIP, csMethod, csUriStem, csUriQuery, csUserAgent, scStatus, csUsername
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Node.js process spawning shell / recon binary (velocityjs SSTI RCE execution) AIExploitation High
Hunts the post-exploitation result of the velocityjs RCE: a node process (node.exe / node) spawning a command shell or reconnaissance binary via child_process.execSync, as in the PoC's execSync('whoami'). A production Node web server rarely shells out to cmd/powershell/sh + whoami, making the parent→child pair high-signal. Rationale: Anchors on the PoC's execution shape — node → child_process.execSync → shell/whoami — using node(.exe) as parent, which a running web server almost never legitimately does for interactive recon binaries. Covers both the article's verified Windows platform and the more common Linux Node deployment. Corroborated by the JS-SSTI child_process technique in PayloadsAllTheThings. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-7gfh-x38p-prh3 • https://github.com/swisskyrepo/PayloadsAllTheThings/blob/master/Server%20Side%20Template%20Injection/JavaScript.md
ATT&CKT1059.003 T1059.004 T1190
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Build/tooling: node running node-gyp, webpack, or npm lifecycle scripts that shell out to cmd/sh
  • Application features that legitimately call child_process (e.g. invoking git, ffmpeg, ImageMagick, or curl) as part of normal workflow
  • Process managers (PM2, forever) or health-check scripts spawning shells
  • DevOps CI runners executing node-based build steps that call whoami/hostname for diagnostics
  • Serverless/container entrypoints where node bootstraps a shell wrapper
Suppression filter
| where not(ProcessCommandLine has_any ("node-gyp","npm","npx","webpack","prebuild","install","git ","\\git.exe"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: examine ProcessCommandLine of the child and InitiatingProcessCommandLine of node — a one-off `cmd /c whoami` / `sh -c whoami` with no build context is suspicious, whereas node-gyp/npm/git command lines are likely benign. Confirm the host runs a public-facing app using velocityjs ≤2.1.6. 2) Contain: isolate the host if the shell ran recon (whoami/ipconfig/net) with no legitimate parent chain; capture the node process command line and open sockets, then rotate any credentials/cloud tokens reachable from the app's environment. 3) Hunt: correlate to the web-layer UC for an inbound constructor.constructor/#set payload just prior; review the node process for subsequent outbound connections (reverse shell / staging), new file writes, and lateral movement from the host.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("node.exe","node")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","whoami.exe","net.exe","net1.exe","hostname.exe","ipconfig.exe","systeminfo.exe","wmic.exe","certutil.exe","bitsadmin.exe","curl.exe","nslookup.exe","sh","bash","dash","whoami","id","uname","curl","wget","nc","ncat")
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, SHA256, InitiatingProcessId, ProcessId
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("node.exe","node")
| where TargetProcessName has_any ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","whoami.exe","net.exe","net1.exe","hostname.exe","ipconfig.exe","systeminfo.exe","wmic.exe","certutil.exe","bitsadmin.exe","curl.exe","nslookup.exe","/sh","/bash","/dash","whoami","uname","wget","ncat")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ParentProcessName, ParentProcessCommandLine, TargetProcessName, TargetProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Vulnerable seroval (<=1.5.2) / TanStack Start (<1.167.30) exposure to CVE-2026-59940 deserialization RCE AIExploitation Medium
Hunts managed assets whose software inventory reports seroval prior to 1.5.3 or @tanstack/start-server-core prior to 1.167.30, the versions vulnerable to the fromJSON() Promise-resolver type-confusion that yields attacker-controlled server-side invocation. The exploit itself is deliberately non-observable in EDR (no PoC published, bypasses request middleware/audit logging and spawns no distinctive child process), so exposure hunting on the concrete package+version is the only reliable article-specific control. Rationale: Uses the exact concrete artifacts the advisory and corroborating sources fix: package `seroval` patched at 1.5.3 (vuln <=1.5.2), downstream `@tanstack/start-server-core` patched at 1.167.30, and CVE-2026-59940. No runtime IOC is emitted because the disclosure explicitly omits the PoC and the exploit bypasses middleware/audit logging with no distinctive process artifact — so exposure hunting is the only article-specific, executable detection. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-mv8w-475r-vwqw • https://cvereports.com/reports/GHSA-9M65-766C-R333 • https://security.snyk.io/vuln/SNYK-JS-SEROVAL-15054506
ATT&CKT1190 T1059.007
Data sources
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Developer/CI/build hosts carrying seroval as a transitive dependency but not running an internet-facing TanStack server function endpoint
  • Assets already remediated but showing stale MDVM inventory before the next scan refresh
  • Bundled/minified copies where the version string is inaccurate or absent, causing over- or under-matching on parse_version
  • Non-server workstations that have the package via an Electron/desktop app with no untrusted-client Seroval JSON ingress
  • Name-collision matches on unrelated software containing the token 'tanstack' or 'seroval' in the display name
Suppression filter
| where not (SoftwareName has "seroval" and parse_version(SoftwareVersion) >= parse_version("1.5.3")) and not (SoftwareName has "tanstack" and parse_version(SoftwareVersion) >= parse_version("1.167.30"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the reported SoftwareVersion is genuinely below the fix (seroval 1.5.3 / start-server-core 1.167.30) and check DeviceInfo.IsInternetFacing plus whether the host actually serves TanStack server functions that deserialize client JSON. 2) Contain: prioritise internet-facing hosts — upgrade to the patched versions and, as defense-in-depth, restrict accepted Seroval node types and allowlist plugin tags for inbound deserialization; isolate any endpoint that cannot be patched immediately. 3) Hunt: on confirmed-exposed hosts review app/WAF logs for POSTs to server-function routes with anomalously large or structurally unusual JSON bodies, and look for any node process spawning unexpected children as a post-deserialization side effect.
// CVE-2026-59940 exposure hunt: vulnerable seroval / TanStack Start server core

| where SoftwareName has "seroval" or SoftwareName has "tanstack"
| extend Ver = parse_version(SoftwareVersion)
| where (SoftwareName has "seroval" and Ver < parse_version("1.5.3"))
     or (SoftwareName has "tanstack" and SoftwareName has_any ("start-server-core","start") and Ver < parse_version("1.167.30"))
| project DeviceName, DeviceId, SoftwareVendor, SoftwareName, SoftwareVersion, OSPlatform
| order by SoftwareName asc

| project TimeGenerated, DeviceName, DeviceId, SoftwareVendor, SoftwareName, SoftwareVersion, CveId, VulnerabilitySeverityLevel, RecommendedSecurityUpdate
| order by DeviceName asc

Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration. → Asset exposure — vulnerability matches article CVE(s)
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad).
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → [LLM] `kiota info` run against a remote/untrusted OpenAPI description (CVE-2026-59865)

`kiota info` run against a remote/untrusted OpenAPI description (CVE-2026-59865) AIExploitation Medium
Surfaces `kiota info` invocations that read an OpenAPI descriptor from a remote/untrusted HTTP(S) source — the precondition for CVE-2026-59865, where a spec-supplied `x-ms-kiota-info.dependencyInstallCommand` replaces kiota's trusted install suggestion and can drive `curl | bash`-style RCE on the developer/CI host. Hunts the kiota process itself with `info` plus a remote `-d`/`--openapi` descriptor rather than a shell child (which the developer or VS Code extension, not kiota, executes). Rationale: Anchors on the article's concrete invocation surface — the `kiota info` subcommand plus a remote `-d`/`--openapi` descriptor — which is the exact vulnerable path (`x-ms-kiota-info.dependencyInstallCommand` is only read/surfaced by `kiota info`). Avoids the unreliable spec-URL field (no such EDR column) and instead pivots on the kiota process image + command line. Cross-checked the GHSA advisory (CVSS 9.3, fixed 1.32.5, PR #7883) and the sibling Kiota CVE-2026-41134 advisory to confirm behaviour and affected packages. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-hq9q-27g5-qwpj • https://github.com/microsoft/kiota/pull/7883 • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-2hx3-vp6r-mg3f
ATT&CKT1059 T1195.001 T1204
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Developer legitimately running `kiota info -d https://<trusted>/openapi.json` against a first-party/internal API spec
  • CI/CD client-generation pipelines that fetch a well-known remote descriptor (e.g. petstore.swagger.io) on every build
  • Platform teams evaluating third-party public APIs where the remote OpenAPI URL is expected
  • kiota invoked via `dotnet kiota` wrapper where the parent, not FileName, carries the 'kiota' token
  • Automated doc/SDK-refresh jobs pulling a partner's hosted OpenAPI description
Suppression filter
| where not (ProcessCommandLine has_any ("petstore.swagger.io", "raw.githubusercontent.com/microsoft", "://localhost", "://127.0.0.1"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the full ProcessCommandLine and resolve the `-d`/`--openapi` URL — is the host untrusted/newly-seen? Confirm the local kiota/VS Code extension version is < 1.32.5 (vulnerable). 2) Contain: on the same host/user within the next few minutes, hunt for a shell running the surfaced install command (`curl`/`wget` piped to `bash`/`sh`, `Invoke-WebRequest`|`IEX`, or `rm -rf`); if found, isolate the workstation/CI runner and reset any dev/cloud/registry credentials reachable from it. 3) Hunt: enumerate all hosts that ran `kiota info` against that URL, block the descriptor domain and any downloaded payload domain, and push the 1.32.5+ upgrade to kiota and the VS Code extension fleet-wide.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName has "kiota" or InitiatingProcessFileName has "kiota"
| where ProcessCommandLine has "info"
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("-d http", "-d https", "--openapi http", "--descriptor http")
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where ActingProcessName has "kiota" or ParentProcessName has "kiota"
| where ActingProcessCommandLine has "info"
| where ActingProcessCommandLine has_any ("-d http", "-d https", "--openapi http", "--descriptor http")
| where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, ParentProcessName, Hash
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Microsoft Kiota APIPlugin manifest generation from OpenAPI spec (CVE-2026-59864) AIWeaponization Medium
Hunts execution of `kiota plugin add` / `kiota plugin generate -t APIPlugin`, the propagation point where an attacker-controlled OpenAPI description's x-ai-adaptive-card / x-ai-capabilities extensions are written verbatim into `<name>-apiplugin.json`. Surfaces the OpenAPI source and kiota version so analysts can confirm whether a poisoned static_template.file path (../ or absolute) was minted. Rationale: Anchors on the article's exact CLI verbs (`plugin add`/`plugin generate`) plus the `APIPlugin` template type and the `kiota` binary (confirmed on the self-contained linux-x64 1.32.4 release; also runs as kiota.exe / `dotnet kiota` on Windows dev hosts). This is the one host-observable event in the chain — where the poisoned static_template.file is emitted. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-4jwf-m4wg-8p66 • https://github.com/microsoft/kiota/pull/7892

  • Engineer following Kiota plugin tutorials/PoC testing
  • Platform team standardising internal API plugins from a vetted spec registry
Suppression filter
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("http://","https://")
Response runbook
1) Triage: inspect the command line's OpenAPI source (`-d`/`--openapi`) — is it a remote URL or third-party/untrusted spec? Confirm the kiota version; 1.32.4 and below are vulnerable, 1.32.5+ is patched. 2) Contain: quarantine the generated `<name>-apiplugin.json`, block its packaging/sideload to Copilot/Teams, and upgrade kiota to 1.32.5+ then regenerate. 3) Hunt: grep all generated manifests for `response_semantics.static_template.file` values containing `../`, absolute paths, UNC (`\\`), Windows drive (`C:\`), or `file://`/`http` URIs; find other plugins built from the same spec source.

Kiota-generated *-apiplugin.json manifest written to disk (CVE-2026-59864 artifact) AIDelivery Medium
Surfaces the write of a `<name>-apiplugin.json` Copilot/Teams plugin manifest by kiota so analysts can open it and inspect the `response_semantics.static_template.file` field for a path/URL-injected traversal (../, absolute, UNC, drive, or file/http URI). This is the exact artifact that carries the CWE-22/CWE-829 payload before it is sideloaded downstream. Rationale: Uses Kiota's fixed output naming convention `<name>-apiplugin.json` (per the advisory) scoped to a kiota/dotnet writer. It hands the analyst the precise file to open and check for a `..`/absolute/UNC/URI static_template.file value — the injected payload — which endpoint file telemetry cannot content-match directly. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-4jwf-m4wg-8p66 • https://github.com/microsoft/kiota/pull/7892
ATT&CKT1195.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate Copilot/Teams plugin builds writing a benign relative static_template.file
  • CI runners regenerating manifests on every commit
  • Developer testing plugin generation locally
  • Repo tooling re-emitting manifests during dependency bumps
Response runbook
1) Triage: open the flagged `-apiplugin.json` and read `functions[].capabilities.response_semantics.static_template.file` — flag if it contains `../`, a leading `/`, `\\`, `C:\`, or a `file://`/`http` URI (patched kiota 1.32.5+ rejects these). 2) Contain: block the manifest from being packaged/sideloaded to Copilot/Teams and upgrade kiota to 1.32.5+, then regenerate from a trusted spec. 3) Hunt: enumerate other `-apiplugin.json` files across build hosts and source repos produced from the same OpenAPI source and re-scan their static_template.file values.

Better-Auth SCIM global user deletion via /scim/v2/Users from unsanctioned caller AIActions on Objectives Medium
Hunts DELETE requests to the better-auth SCIM Users endpoint (/scim/v2/Users/:id) coming from a source IP that has never previously driven SCIM traffic. On affected @better-auth/scim (>=1.4.0-beta.27 <=1.6.21, 1.7.0-beta.0-9) a low-privileged authenticated user can mint a SCIM token with a colliding provider ID and DELETE the global Better Auth user plus sessions. Legitimate SCIM deprovisioning originates from the IdP's fixed egress; a delete from a fresh caller IP is the collision-abuse signal. Rationale: Uses the exact endpoint string from the advisory (DELETE /scim/v2/Users/:id — the highest-impact non-org deletion path) and the baseline anti-join on caller IP to separate colliding-token abuse from legitimate IdP deprovisioning, which always comes from a fixed egress. No endpoint/EDR telemetry exists for an inbound HTTP authz flaw, so only web-log platforms are populated. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-rjg6-39jm-rgg4 • https://advisories.gitlab.com/npm/@better-auth/scim/GHSA-rjg6-39jm-rgg4/ • https://better-auth.com/docs/plugins/scim
ATT&CKT1531 T1550.001
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate IdP (Entra/Okta) deprovisioning from a newly rotated egress IP not seen in the 30d baseline
  • IdP failover to a secondary datacenter with a different public IP
  • Scheduled SCIM connector migrated to a new host/IP
  • Authorized penetration test or SCIM integration testing against the endpoint
  • Admin manually calling the SCIM API from a jump host during troubleshooting
Response runbook
1) Triage: Pull the DELETE events; identify the caller IP, csUserName, User-Agent and the /Users/:id targets; confirm the IP is NOT your sanctioned IdP egress and decode the SCIM bearer token's provider ID to see if it collides with an SSO/OIDC/OAuth/social provider namespace. 2) Contain: Revoke the offending SCIM token, disable SCIM token generation (canGenerateToken) for non-privileged users, block the source IP, and restore deleted users/sessions from backup. 3) Hunt: Audit scimProvider rows for providerId values matching other account providers, review PUT/PATCH activity on the same endpoint from the same caller, and upgrade to @better-auth/scim 1.6.22 or 1.7.0-beta.10.
// Baseline = IPs that legitimately drove SCIM in the prior 30d (your IdP egress)
let SanctionedScimCallers = W3CIISLog
    | where TimeGenerated between (ago(30d) .. ago(1d))
    | where csUriStem has "/scim/v2/Users"
    | summarize by cIP;
W3CIISLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where csUriStem has "/scim/v2/Users"
| where csMethod == "DELETE"
| where scStatus in (200, 204)            // successful global-user deletion
| join kind=leftanti SanctionedScimCallers on cIP   // delete from an IP never before seen issuing SCIM
| project TimeGenerated, cIP, csUserName, csMethod, csUriStem, scStatus, csUserAgent, sSiteName, Computer, sPort
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Better-Auth SCIM profile/email rewrite fan-out across many /scim/v2/Users resources AIActions on Objectives Medium
Hunts a single caller issuing PUT/PATCH updates against many distinct better-auth SCIM Users resources (/scim/v2/Users/:id). On affected @better-auth/scim, a colliding-provider-ID token can resolve SSO/OIDC-provisioned users it never provisioned and rewrite global profile fields; SCIM PUT/PATCH also changed email without the create-path uniqueness check and left emailVerified stale — enabling account takeover. A colliding token enumerating and rewriting >5 distinct user resources is the fan-out signal. Rationale: Targets the advisory's second write path — PUT/PATCH to /scim/v2/Users rewriting global email/profile fields via a colliding provider ID. dcount over distinct /Users/:id paths captures the enumerate-and-rewrite fan-out that separates one caller mutating many unowned users from a normal single-target IdP update. Threshold-based, so no Sigma emitted. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-rjg6-39jm-rgg4 • https://advisories.gitlab.com/npm/@better-auth/scim/GHSA-rjg6-39jm-rgg4/ • https://better-auth.com/docs/plugins/scim
ATT&CKT1098 T1550.001
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • IdP bulk attribute sync (job title/department/manager) touching many users after an HR data change
  • Initial SCIM provisioning backfill writing all existing users at onboarding
  • IdP re-sync following a SCIM connector configuration change or schema update
  • IdP retry storm re-issuing PUT/PATCH after a transient failure
  • Scheduled reconciliation job that periodically re-pushes all mapped attributes
Response runbook
1) Triage: Identify the caller IP/csUserName and enumerate which /Users/:id resources were modified; decode the SCIM token provider ID and check whether it collides with an SSO/OIDC/OAuth/social provider namespace the caller does not own. 2) Contain: Revoke the SCIM token, restrict canGenerateToken, and for any user whose email was reassigned force emailVerified reset + password/session reset to block takeover of email-keyed login. 3) Hunt: Correlate with DELETE activity on the same endpoint, audit scimProvider rows for colliding providerId, verify no duplicate/hijacked email addresses were created, and upgrade to 1.6.22 / 1.7.0-beta.10.
W3CIISLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where csUriStem has "/scim/v2/Users"
| where csMethod in ("PUT", "PATCH")
| where scStatus between (200 .. 299)
| summarize WriteCount = count(),
            DistinctUserResources = dcount(csUriStem),
            Methods = make_set(csMethod),
            UserAgents = make_set(csUserAgent, 5),
            FirstSeen = min(TimeGenerated),
            LastSeen = max(TimeGenerated)
            by cIP, csUserName, sSiteName
| where DistinctUserResources > 5     // one caller rewriting >5 distinct /Users/:id resources = collision fan-out
| order by WriteCount desc

msaRAT: MSI impersonating Windows update executed from ProgramData AIInstallation High
Hunts msiexec.exe executing an MSI dropped to C:\ProgramData whose name/property info impersonates a Windows update, matching Chaos ransomware's msaRAT delivery where a custom action loads the RAT DLL straight into memory. Article-specific: the installer masquerades as a Windows update and lives in ProgramData rather than a signed update path. Rationale: Uses the article's exact delivery: an MSI in ProgramData impersonating a Windows update executed by msiexec, with a memory-loading custom action. Cross-checked against Talos full report and The Hacker News which confirm the installer property info impersonates a Windows update. Cross-checked against: • https://blog.talosintelligence.com/chaos-msarat-living-off-the-browser-to-build-covert-c2-channel/ • https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/chaos-ransomware-uses-msarat-to-route.html
ATT&CKT1218.007 T1036.005 T1204.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Third-party software packaged as an MSI staged in ProgramData by a legitimate installer bootstrapper
  • Enterprise software distribution (SCCM/Intune) caching update MSIs under ProgramData vendor folders
  • Driver/firmware update utilities (Dell, Lenovo, HP) that stage MSIs named with 'Update' in ProgramData
  • Legitimate Windows optional-feature MSIs referenced with KB numbers in command line
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("ccmexec.exe","tiworker.exe","trustedinstaller.exe") and InitiatingProcessFolderPath has @"\Windows\")
Response runbook
1) Triage: Pull the full msiexec command line and the MSI file hash; check the parent process and whether the MSI is signed and by whom (msaRAT installer is unsigned/impersonates Windows). Query DeviceImageLoadEvents for a DLL loaded by msiexec.exe from ProgramData at the same time. 2) Contain: Isolate the host, kill the msiexec/child process tree, and block the MSI hash org-wide. 3) Hunt: Look on the same host for a preceding curl.exe download to ProgramData and subsequent headless chrome.exe/msedge.exe launched with --remote-debugging flags (msaRAT CDP C2).
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName =~ "msiexec.exe"
| where ProcessCommandLine has @"\ProgramData\"
| where ProcessCommandLine has ".msi"
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("update","kb","patch","windows")
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where NewProcessName endswith "\\msiexec.exe"
| where CommandLine has "\\ProgramData\\"
| where CommandLine has ".msi"
| where CommandLine has_any ("update","kb","patch","windows")
| where SubjectUserName !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, NewProcessName, CommandLine, ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

msaRAT: curl.exe downloading MSI payload into ProgramData AIDelivery High
Detects curl.exe (or wget) retrieving a .msi to C:\ProgramData, the exact ingress step Talos describes for Chaos ransomware's msaRAT before the fake Windows-update installer runs. Article-specific: correlates the curl download with the msaRAT delivery IP 172.86.126.18 and the workers.dev signaling infra. Rationale: Directly implements Talos's 'monitor for unusual curl commands downloading MSI files to ProgramData' guidance, anchored on the confirmed delivery IP 172.86.126.18 and the workers.dev signaling domain. Corroborated by The Hacker News and Help Net Security. Cross-checked against: • https://blog.talosintelligence.com/chaos-msarat-living-off-the-browser-to-build-covert-c2-channel/ • https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/chaos-ransomware-uses-msarat-to-route.html • https://www.helpnetsecurity.com/2026/07/23/cisco-talos-chaos-ransomware-msarat/
ATT&CKT1105
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Developer or DevOps scripts using curl to fetch MSI installers into a working directory under ProgramData
  • Software packaging/CI agents downloading MSI artifacts to a ProgramData staging cache
  • Admin manually fetching a vendor MSI with curl for testing
  • Chocolatey/winget-style tooling that shells out to curl for package retrieval
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("choco.exe","winget.exe") and ProcessCommandLine has "workers.dev" == false)
Response runbook
1) Triage: Extract the full download URL from the curl command line and check reputation of the host/IP; confirm the destination path in ProgramData and whether the resulting MSI was subsequently executed by msiexec. 2) Contain: Isolate the host, block the URL/IP (172.86.126.18) and workers.dev signaling domain at proxy/firewall, and quarantine the downloaded MSI. 3) Hunt: Search the host and org for the same URL/IP in DeviceNetworkEvents and for a following headless browser launch with --remote-debugging (msaRAT C2 stage).
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName in~ ("curl.exe","wget.exe")
| where ProcessCommandLine has ".msi"
| where ProcessCommandLine has @"\ProgramData\" or ProcessCommandLine has_any ("172.86.126.18","workers.dev")
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where NewProcessName endswith "\\curl.exe" or NewProcessName endswith "\\wget.exe"
| where CommandLine has ".msi"
| where CommandLine has "\\ProgramData\\" or CommandLine has_any ("172.86.126.18","workers.dev")
| where SubjectUserName !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, NewProcessName, CommandLine, ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: msaRAT curl Download of MSI to ProgramData

msaRAT: Headless Chrome/Edge launched with remote-debugging (CDP abuse) AICommand & Control Medium
Hunts chrome.exe/msedge.exe spawned with --remote-debugging-port/--remote-debugging-pipe (and typically --headless) by a non-interactive parent, the mechanism msaRAT uses to drive a browser over the Chrome DevTools Protocol for covert C2. Article-specific: the RAT starts its own headless browser instance and controls it via CDP rather than touching the network directly. Rationale: Targets the CDP-driven headless browser msaRAT spawns for C2 (Talos: 'implement behavioral monitoring to catch Chrome DevTools Protocol abuse'). Confirmed by BleepingComputer and The Hacker News that the RAT starts Chrome/Edge in headless mode and drives it over CDP. Cross-checked against: • https://blog.talosintelligence.com/chaos-msarat-living-off-the-browser-to-build-covert-c2-channel/ • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/new-msarat-malware-uses-chrome-edge-browsers-to-route-c2-traffic/ • https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/chaos-ransomware-uses-msarat-to-route.html
ATT&CKT1205 T1071.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Automated browser testing frameworks (Puppeteer, Playwright, Selenium headless) run by developers or CI runners
  • PDF-generation or web-scraping services that drive headless Chromium
  • Lighthouse/synthetic-monitoring agents launching headless Edge/Chrome
  • Electron-based apps invoking a bundled Chromium with debugging pipe
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("node.exe","pwsh.exe","python.exe") and InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("puppeteer","playwright","selenium","lighthouse"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: Identify the parent process that launched the headless browser and its binary path/signature; a browser started by an unsigned/unknown parent (not a dev tool, IDE, or CI agent) is high-suspicion. Check for a co-occurring loopback (127.0.0.1) debugging listener. 2) Contain: If the parent is untrusted, isolate the host and kill the browser + parent tree. 3) Hunt: Pivot from the host to DeviceNetworkEvents for browser egress to workers.dev / STUN (3478) / Twilio TURN, and back to any preceding msiexec-from-ProgramData execution.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe")
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("--remote-debugging-port","--remote-debugging-pipe")
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| extend Headless = ProcessCommandLine has "--headless"
| where Headless or InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("explorer.exe","chrome.exe","msedge.exe","userinit.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, Headless, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFolderPath
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where NewProcessName endswith "\\chrome.exe" or NewProcessName endswith "\\msedge.exe"
| where CommandLine has_any ("--remote-debugging-port","--remote-debugging-pipe")
| where SubjectUserName !endswith "$"
| extend Headless = CommandLine has "--headless"
| where Headless or ParentProcessName !endswith "\\explorer.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, NewProcessName, CommandLine, Headless, ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: Headless Browser Launched with Remote Debugging (msaRAT CDP C2)

msaRAT: Connection to Chaos delivery IP / workers.dev signaling relay AICommand & Control Medium
Alerts on any host connecting to the msaRAT delivery server 172.86.126.18 (plain HTTP over port 443) or the Cloudflare workers.dev signaling relay is-01-ast.ols-img-12.workers.dev. Article-specific: these are the confirmed network IOCs for msaRAT's payload delivery and WebRTC signaling. Rationale: Direct IOC match on the confirmed msaRAT delivery server (172.86.126.18, plain HTTP over 443) and the workers.dev signaling relay, both published in the Talos report and echoed by Security Affairs/Help Net Security. High-fidelity, low-FP IOC alert. Cross-checked against: • https://blog.talosintelligence.com/chaos-msarat-living-off-the-browser-to-build-covert-c2-channel/ • https://securityaffairs.com/195876/malware/chaos-ransomware-deploys-browser-based-msarat-to-evade-network-detection.html • https://www.helpnetsecurity.com/2026/07/23/cisco-talos-chaos-ransomware-msarat/
ATT&CKT1572 T1090.001
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Benign traffic to an unrelated tenant sharing the ols-img-12.workers.dev Cloudflare Worker subdomain (unlikely but possible if the subdomain is later repurposed)
  • Security tooling / sandbox detonating the sample and generating IOC contact from a research host
  • Threat-intel enrichment or IOC-validation scanners in the environment reaching the IP
  • Stale IOC after infrastructure takedown produces sinkhole hits
Response runbook
1) Triage: Identify the initiating process — a browser (chrome/msedge) reaching workers.dev or any process reaching 172.86.126.18 on 443; confirm whether traffic to the IP is plain HTTP despite the 443 port (protocol mismatch is a strong indicator). 2) Contain: Block the IP and domain at the perimeter, isolate the host, and capture the process tree. 3) Hunt: On the host, look for the preceding curl→ProgramData MSI download, msiexec fake-update execution, and a headless browser launched with --remote-debugging; sweep the org for any other host that contacted either IOC.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RemoteIP == "172.86.126.18" or RemoteUrl =~ "is-01-ast.ols-img-12.workers.dev"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, RemoteIP, RemotePort, RemoteUrl, Protocol
| order by Timestamp desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where DstIpAddr == "172.86.126.18" or DstHostname =~ "is-01-ast.ols-img-12.workers.dev" or Url has "is-01-ast.ols-img-12.workers.dev"
| project TimeGenerated, SrcHostname, SrcIpAddr, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber, DstHostname, NetworkApplicationProtocol, Url
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: msaRAT Delivery IP / workers.dev Signaling Relay Contact

msaRAT: Headless browser initiating WebRTC STUN/TURN egress AICommand & Control Medium
Hunts chrome.exe/msedge.exe making STUN/TURN connections (ports 3478/5349) when the browser was launched non-interactively with debugging/headless flags — the WebRTC data-channel egress msaRAT relays through Twilio TURN for C2. Article-specific: msaRAT sends a STUN request then tunnels C2 over WebRTC from its own headless browser, not user-driven WebRTC. Rationale: Targets msaRAT's WebRTC egress (STUN request + Twilio TURN relay) constrained to a headless/CDP-driven browser so it isn't just generic WebRTC noise. Talos, BleepingComputer and The Hacker News confirm the STUN-then-WebRTC-via-Twilio C2 path. Cross-checked against: • https://blog.talosintelligence.com/chaos-msarat-living-off-the-browser-to-build-covert-c2-channel/ • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/new-msarat-malware-uses-chrome-edge-browsers-to-route-c2-traffic/
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1572
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate video conferencing / VoIP in-browser (Google Meet, Teams web, Discord web) using WebRTC STUN/TURN
  • Browser-based screen-sharing or WebRTC test pages initiated by a user
  • Puppeteer/Playwright automation that legitimately exercises WebRTC
  • Corporate SBC/collaboration platforms relaying media over 3478/5349
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessParentFileName in~ ("teams.exe","ms-teams.exe","slack.exe","discord.exe") )
Response runbook
1) Triage: Confirm the browser was launched non-interactively (parent is not explorer.exe and command line carries --headless/--remote-debugging); user-driven Meet/Teams WebRTC will have an interactive parent and no debugging flags. 2) Contain: If non-interactive, isolate the host, kill the browser + parent, and block the TURN destination and the workers.dev signaling domain. 3) Hunt: Correlate on the host with the CDP browser-launch detection, contact to 172.86.126.18 / workers.dev, and the fake-update MSI chain; check for Chaos ransomware staging (shadow-copy deletion, RMM tools).
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe")
| where RemotePort in (3478, 5349)
| where InitiatingProcessParentFileName !in~ ("explorer.exe","chrome.exe","msedge.exe","userinit.exe","svchost.exe")
| where InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("--headless","--remote-debugging-port","--remote-debugging-pipe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessParentFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Protocol
| order by Timestamp desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where DstPortNumber in (3478, 5349)
| where NetworkProtocol has_any ("UDP","TCP")
| project TimeGenerated, SrcHostname, SrcIpAddr, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber, NetworkProtocol, NetworkApplicationProtocol
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations Command & Control Medium
C2 channel detection via inter-beacon-time stddev / fan-out to single dest.
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1071.004
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where RemoteIPType == "Public" and ActionType == "ConnectionSuccess"
| project DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Timestamp
| sort by DeviceName asc, RemoteIP asc, RemotePort asc, Timestamp asc
| extend prev_dev = prev(DeviceName, 1), prev_ip = prev(RemoteIP, 1),
         prev_port = prev(RemotePort, 1), prev_ts = prev(Timestamp, 1)
| where DeviceName == prev_dev and RemoteIP == prev_ip and RemotePort == prev_port
| extend delta_sec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, prev_ts)
| summarize conn_count = count(), avg_delta = avg(delta_sec), stdev_delta = stdev(delta_sec)
    by DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| where conn_count > 30 and avg_delta between (30.0 .. 600.0) and stdev_delta < 5.0
| order by conn_count desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(2h)
| where DvcAction != "Block"
| where ipv4_is_private(DstIpAddr) == false
| summarize ConnCount = count(),
            DistinctMinutes = dcount(bin(TimeGenerated, 1m))
            by DvcHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber
| where ConnCount > 50 and DistinctMinutes > 30   // sustained, not bursty
| order by ConnCount desc
NETWORK
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count, values(All_Traffic.dest_port) AS ports
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
    where All_Traffic.action="allowed" AND All_Traffic.dest_category!="internal"
    by _time span=10s, All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| streamstats current=f last(_time) AS prev_time by src, dest
| eval delta = _time - prev_time
| stats avg(delta) AS avg_delta stdev(delta) AS sd_delta count by src, dest
| where count > 30 AND sd_delta < 5 AND avg_delta>=30 AND avg_delta<=600
| sort - count
| tstats summariesonly=false count, values(All_Traffic.dest_port) AS ports
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
    where All_Traffic.action="allowed" AND All_Traffic.dest_category!="internal"
    by _time span=10s, All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| streamstats current=f last(_time) AS prev_time by src, dest
| eval delta = _time - prev_time
| stats avg(delta) AS avg_delta stdev(delta) AS sd_delta count by src, dest
| where count > 30 AND sd_delta < 5 AND avg_delta>=30 AND avg_delta<=600
| sort - count
Network connections to article IPs / domains Command & Control High

title: Outbound Connection to Article-Named IP / Domain
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d0f
status: experimental
description: |

detection:
    selection_ip:

            - '__IP_PLACEHOLDER_2__'
    selection_domain:

            - '__DOMAIN_PLACEHOLDER_2__'

NETWORK
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.

     | `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`]
| append
    [| tstats summariesonly=false count from datamodel=Network_Resolution.DNS

Asset exposure — vulnerability matches article CVE(s) Reconnaissance High
Match vulnerability scanner output to the CVE(s) named in the article.
ATT&CKT1190
Data sourcesVulnerabilities DeviceInfo DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
// TVM tables are daily snapshots — pin a 1-day window so the engine
// partitions on Timestamp instead of scanning the full retention.
DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where CveId in~ ("CVE-2026-60137", "CVE-2026-63030")
| join kind=inner (DeviceInfo | where Timestamp > ago(1d)) on DeviceId
| project DeviceName, OSPlatform, CveId, VulnerabilitySeverityLevel, RecommendedSecurityUpdate
| order by VulnerabilitySeverityLevel asc, DeviceName asc

// Sentinel has no native TVM table. If MDE→Sentinel streaming is enabled,
// `DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities` is available. Otherwise this UC has
// no Sentinel translation — track via Update / Heartbeat OS-version
// gaps as a coarse approximation.
DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where CveId in~ ("CVE-2026-60137", "CVE-2026-63030")
| join kind=inner (DeviceInfo | where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)) on DeviceId
| project DeviceName, OSPlatform, CveId,
          VulnerabilitySeverityLevel, RecommendedSecurityUpdate
| order by VulnerabilitySeverityLevel asc, DeviceName asc
APPLICATION
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Vulnerabilities
    where Vulnerabilities.signature IN ("CVE-2026-60137", "CVE-2026-63030")
    by Vulnerabilities.dest, Vulnerabilities.signature, Vulnerabilities.severity, Vulnerabilities.cve
| `drop_dm_object_name(Vulnerabilities)`
| sort - severity
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Vulnerabilities
    where Vulnerabilities.signature IN ("CVE-2026-60137", "CVE-2026-63030")
    by Vulnerabilities.dest, Vulnerabilities.signature, Vulnerabilities.severity, Vulnerabilities.cve
| `drop_dm_object_name(Vulnerabilities)`
| sort - severity
Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change Actions on Objectives Medium
Threshold detection: many files renamed in short window, often with new extension.
ATT&CKT1486
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem DeviceFileEvents
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(FileName) by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, bin(Timestamp, 1m)
| where files > 200    // empirical: > 200 unique-file renames in 1m by one account on one host
                       //            is well above the P99 of legitimate bulk-tooling
| order by files desc

ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
| where EventType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(TargetFileName)
            by DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, bin(TimeGenerated, 1m)
| where files > 200    // P99 of legit bulk-tooling per-minute rename volume
| order by files desc
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count, dc(Filesystem.file_name) AS files
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where Filesystem.action IN ("modified","renamed")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.user, _time span=1m
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| where files > 200
| sort - files
| tstats summariesonly=false count, dc(Filesystem.file_name) AS files
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where Filesystem.action IN ("modified","renamed")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.user, _time span=1m
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| where files > 200
| sort - files
LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) Actions on Objectives High
Mimikatz, comsvcs.dll MiniDump, or any non-Windows process opening LSASS.
ATT&CKT1003.001 T1003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceEvents
DeviceEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType == "OpenProcessApiCall"
| where FileName =~ "lsass.exe"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("MsSense.exe","MsMpEng.exe","csrss.exe",
                                          "svchost.exe","wininit.exe","services.exe",
                                          "lsm.exe","SearchProtocolHost.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFolderPath, AccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
// SecurityEvent EventID 4663 = object access. AccessMask 0x10 / 0x40 / 0x1010
// indicate read access to lsass.exe — credential-dump signature. Audit
// Object Access > Audit File System policy required.
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4663
| where ObjectName endswith "\lsass.exe"
| where Account !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ObjectName, ProcessName,
          AccessMask, AccessReason
| order by TimeGenerated desc

title: LSASS Process Access Outside Microsoft-Signed Tooling
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d04
status: experimental
description: |
    Anything opening lsass.exe with read-memory access that isn't a
    Microsoft signed component (Defender, csrss, etc.) is suspect.
    Mimikatz / Pypykatz / nanodump signature.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1003/001/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1003.001
    - attack.credential-access
logsource:
    category: process_access
    product: windows
detection:
    selection:
        TargetImage|endswith: '\lsass.exe'
    filter_known_good:
        SourceImage|endswith:
            - '\MsSense.exe'
            - '\MsMpEng.exe'
            - '\csrss.exe'
            - '\svchost.exe'
            - '\wininit.exe'
            - '\services.exe'
            - '\lsm.exe'
            - '\SearchProtocolHost.exe'
    condition: selection and not filter_known_good
falsepositives:
    - Third-party EDR / forensic tools — extend the filter list
level: high
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where (Processes.process="*lsass*" OR Processes.process="*sekurlsa*"
        OR Processes.process="*MiniDump*" OR Processes.process="*comsvcs.dll*MiniDump*"
        OR Processes.process="*procdump*lsass*")
       OR (Processes.process_name="rundll32.exe" AND Processes.process="*comsvcs*MiniDump*")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process_name, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where (Processes.process="*lsass*" OR Processes.process="*sekurlsa*"
        OR Processes.process="*MiniDump*" OR Processes.process="*comsvcs.dll*MiniDump*"
        OR Processes.process="*procdump*lsass*")
       OR (Processes.process_name="rundll32.exe" AND Processes.process="*comsvcs*MiniDump*")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process_name, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
Remote service execution — PsExec / SMB lateral movement Actions on Objectives High
psexec / paexec / smbexec / wmic /node — service install over SMB from remote host.
ATT&CKT1021.002 T1569.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceProcessEvents
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where FileName in~ ("psexec.exe","psexesvc.exe","paexec.exe","smbexec.py")
   or (FileName =~ "wmic.exe" and ProcessCommandLine has "/node:")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName

SecurityEvent

| where Account !endswith "$"

   or NewProcessName endswith "\psexesvc.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\paexec.exe"
   or (NewProcessName endswith "\wmic.exe" and CommandLine has "/node:")

          ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

title: PsExec / SMB Lateral Movement Tooling Execution
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d03
status: experimental
description: |
    PsExec, paexec, smbexec, csexec, remcom — admin-grade tooling that
    pivots over SMB. Pair with `wmic /node:` for the full cluster.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1021/002/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1569/002/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1021.002
    - attack.t1569.002
    - attack.lateral-movement
    - attack.execution
logsource:
    category: process_creation
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_psexec:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\psexec.exe'
            - '\psexec64.exe'
            - '\psexesvc.exe'
            - '\paexec.exe'
            - '\csexec.exe'
            - '\remcom.exe'
            - '\smbexec.py'
    selection_wmic_remote:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\wmic.exe'
        CommandLine|contains:
            - '/node:'
    condition: selection_psexec or selection_wmic_remote
falsepositives:
    - Sysadmins running approved remote-management tooling — wrap with
      a known-admin-host watchlist
level: high
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.process_name IN ("psexec.exe","psexesvc.exe","paexec.exe","smbexec.py")
       OR (Processes.process_name="wmic.exe" AND Processes.process="*/node:*")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process_name, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.process_name IN ("psexec.exe","psexesvc.exe","paexec.exe","smbexec.py")
       OR (Processes.process_name="wmic.exe" AND Processes.process="*/node:*")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process_name, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
Trusted vendor binary / installer launching unusual children Exploitation Medium
Supply-chain trojan signal: legitimate signed binary spawning script interpreters or exotic LOLBins.
ATT&CKT1195.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceProcessEvents
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("setup.exe","installer.exe","update.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","cmd.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","mshta.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","wmic.exe","bitsadmin.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine
// Replace `"setup.exe","installer.exe","update.exe"` with the vendor binaries observed in the
// article (matching shape with the Defender query).
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where Account !endswith "$"
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("setup.exe","installer.exe","update.exe")
| where NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\rundll32.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\regsvr32.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wmic.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\bitsadmin.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

title: Trusted Vendor Binary Launching Unusual Children
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d09
status: experimental
description: |
    A signed vendor binary (in the article's named-vendors list)
    spawning script-host or LOLBin children. Strongest signal when
    paired with a recent CVE / supply-chain advisory naming the same
    vendor.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1195/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1195
    - attack.initial-access
logsource:
    category: process_creation
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_child:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\powershell.exe'
            - '\pwsh.exe'
            - '\cmd.exe'
            - '\rundll32.exe'
            - '\regsvr32.exe'
            - '\mshta.exe'
            - '\wscript.exe'
            - '\cscript.exe'
            - '\wmic.exe'
            - '\bitsadmin.exe'
    selection_parent_vendor:
        ParentImage|contains:
            - '\Program Files\'
            - '\Program Files (x86)\'
    condition: selection_child and selection_parent_vendor

      the parent path to specific vendor binaries observed in the
      article before alerting.
level: medium
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("setup.exe","installer.exe","update.exe")
      AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","cmd.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","mshta.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","wmic.exe","bitsadmin.exe")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("setup.exe","installer.exe","update.exe")
      AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","cmd.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","mshta.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","wmic.exe","bitsadmin.exe")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match Installation High
Match SHA256/SHA1/MD5 named in the article against EDR file/process telemetry.
ATT&CKT1027
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem Endpoint.Processes DeviceFileEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Pre-filter each table BEFORE the union — the engine cannot push
// predicates across `union`, and DeviceFileEvents lacks ProcessCommandLine
// (Initiating only) so column-projection has to differ per side.
union
    ( DeviceFileEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)

    ( ImFileEvent
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where TargetFileSHA256 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileSHA1 in~ (BadHashes)

                  TargetFileSHA256 = SHA256,
                  Cmd = TargetProcessCommandLine, Source = "ImProcessCreate" )
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Email threat landscape: Q2 2026 trends and insights

Microsoft Security Blog
2026-07-23 14 use cases 6 techniques 6 kill-chain phases detected

In the second quarter of 2026, the continuing effects of Microsoft’s disruption of the Tycoon2FA phishing platform contributed to sustained declines in several major phishing techniques, while threat actors expanded into Teams-based social engineering and employed increasingly automated and multi-stage attack chains. The post Email threat landscape: Q2 2026 trends and insights appeared first on Microsoft Security Blog .

Actions on Objectives
Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → [LLM] Inbound phishing from BEC sender domain 9i6pokerdepot.com (Q2 2026 ClickUp/pixeldrain chain) · [LLM] Financial_report.bat dropper downloaded from ClickUp attachment host · Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution · Email attachment opened from external sender · Microsoft Teams external-tenant chat from unverified IT-helpdesk impersonator
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → Office app spawning script/LOLBin child process · Fake CAPTCHA / clipboard-injected PowerShell (ClickFix / FakeCaptcha) · PowerShell encoded / obfuscated command · Article-specific behavioural hunt — Email threat landscape: Q2 2026 trends and insights
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] Hidden PowerShell pulls installer.exe from pixeldrain.com to %Temp% (self-deleting dropper) · RMM tool installed by non-IT user — remote-access utility for hands-on-keyboard
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → [LLM] Network/DNS contact to Q2 2026 campaign infrastructure (pixeldrain payload + ClickUp dropper hosts) · Network connections to article IPs / domains
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → OAuth consent / suspicious app grant
Inbound phishing from BEC sender domain 9i6pokerdepot.com (Q2 2026 ClickUp/pixeldrain chain) AIDelivery High
Hunts inbound email from the DKIM-signed operator domain 9i6pokerdepot.com (sender Customer.Service@9i6pokerdepot.com) used in Microsoft's Q2 2026 multi-stage campaign that lured users with a fake 'Internal Affairs – Financials & Staff Updates' message. This is the delivery anchor of the chain that ends in silent malware execution via ClickUp and pixeldrain. Rationale: Anchors on the exact sender domain (9i6pokerdepot.com) and full address (Customer.Service@9i6pokerdepot.com) from the article's IOC table; a niche gambling-themed domain sending to enterprise mailboxes is effectively zero-FP. Cross-checked against: • https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/security/blog/2026/07/23/email-threat-landscape-q2-2026-trends-and-insights/ • https://cybersecuritynews.com/email-phishing-threats-as-teams-vishing-attacks/
ATT&CKT1566.001 T1656
Data sourcesEmail
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A security team deliberately replays the IOC domain in a phishing-simulation/purple-team exercise
  • Threat-intel or sandbox tooling that re-sends captured campaign samples into a test mailbox
  • A researcher forwarding the original email internally for analysis (appears as intra-org, not inbound)
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull all recipients of the message via NetworkMessageId; check DeliveryLocation (Inbox vs Quarantine) and whether any user opened it. 2) Contain: soft-delete/purge the message tenant-wide with an EmailPostDelivery/ZAP action and block 9i6pokerdepot.com at the mail gateway and Safe Links. 3) Hunt: for every recipient, pivot to UC2/UC3 — look for Financial_report.bat writes and PowerShell contacting pixeldrain.com on their devices in the following 24h.
EmailEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
| where SenderMailFromDomain =~ "9i6pokerdepot.com" or SenderFromDomain =~ "9i6pokerdepot.com" or SenderFromAddress =~ "customer.service@9i6pokerdepot.com"
| project Timestamp, NetworkMessageId, SenderFromAddress, SenderMailFromAddress, SenderDisplayName, RecipientEmailAddress, Subject, DeliveryAction, DeliveryLocation, AuthenticationDetails
| order by Timestamp desc

| project TimeGenerated, NetworkMessageId, SenderFromAddress, SenderMailFromAddress, SenderDisplayName, RecipientEmailAddress, Subject, DeliveryAction, DeliveryLocation, AuthenticationDetails
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Financial_report.bat dropper downloaded from ClickUp attachment host AIDelivery High
Detects the stage-2 batch dropper (Financial_report.bat) written to disk with a download origin of clickup-attachments.com — the trusted-service hop the Q2 2026 campaign used after a login.microsoftonline.com redirect. ClickUp's public attachment host serving a .bat file is the article-specific tell. Rationale: Uses the exact dropper filename (Financial_report.bat) and the trusted-service host (clickup-attachments.com, subdomain t90141296286.p.clickup-attachments.com) from the article and corroborating write-up; a .bat sourced from ClickUp is not a legitimate business pattern. Cross-checked against: • https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/security/blog/2026/07/23/email-threat-landscape-q2-2026-trends-and-insights/ • https://cybersecuritynews.com/email-phishing-threats-as-teams-vishing-attacks/
ATT&CKT1105 T1608.001 T1204.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem Web.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A dev team legitimately storing build/automation .bat scripts as ClickUp task attachments and downloading them
  • IR/malware analyst intentionally downloading the sample from ClickUp for analysis
  • Generic '.bat in %Temp%' branch firing on an installer's own temporary batch helper (mitigated by the clickup-attachments.com origin clause on the primary path)
Suppression filter

Response runbook
1) Triage: on the flagged host, capture the SHA256 of Financial_report.bat and the InitiatingProcess (browser/Outlook) that wrote it; confirm the FileOriginUrl subdomain. 2) Contain: isolate the host if the .bat already executed (check for cmd.exe→powershell.exe children); block clickup-attachments.com download paths at proxy and delete the file. 3) Hunt: pivot to UC3 — search DeviceProcessEvents on the same host/user for PowerShell referencing pixeldrain.com and installer.exe in %Temp%.

| where FileName =~ "Financial_report.bat" or FileName endswith ".bat"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256, FileOriginUrl, FileOriginReferrerUrl, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
ImWebSession

| project TimeGenerated, SrcIpAddr, SrcHostname, SrcUsername, Url, FileName, HttpUserAgent = HttpRequestHeaderUserAgent, DvcAction

Hidden PowerShell pulls installer.exe from pixeldrain.com to %Temp% (self-deleting dropper) AIInstallation High
Detects the final-stage behaviour of the Q2 2026 chain: Financial_report.bat spawning a hidden PowerShell that downloads installer.exe from pixeldrain.com into the user's Temp directory, runs it with a silent flag, then deletes the dropper. Anchored on the pixeldrain download string in a hidden-window PowerShell command line. Rationale: Combines the concrete C2/payload host (pixeldrain.com, file id 3v92oJiL) and behaviour (hidden PowerShell fetching installer.exe into %Temp%) from the article plus the corroborating write-up; pixeldrain in a PowerShell download command line is a high-fidelity, near-zero-FP signal.
